question.prompt: Let \(n\) be the number of integer values of \(x\) such that \(P=x^4+6x^3+11x^2+3x+31\) is the square of an integer. Then \(n\) is:

solutions.explanation:
The leading terms suggest looking for the square of a quadratic. In fact,
\[
(x^2+3x+1)^2=x^4+6x^3+11x^2+6x+1.
\]
Thus, if \(q=x^2+3x+1\), then
\[
P=q^2+30-3x.
\]
The remainder is only linear, which makes it possible to trap \(P\) between nearby integer squares outside a small range.

If \(x\leq-7\), put \(t=-x\geq7\). Then \(q=t(t-3)+1\geq29\), and \(P>q^2\). Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(q+1)^2-P
&=2t^2-9t-27\\
&=t(2t-9)-27\\
&\geq7\cdot5-27=8>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(q^2<P<(q+1)^2\), so \(P\) is not an integer square.

If \(x\geq3\), then \(q\geq19\). We have
\[
P-(q-1)^2=2x^2+3x+31>0
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
(q+1)^2-P
&=2x^2+9x-27\\
&=2x^2+9(x-3)>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence \((q-1)^2<P<(q+1)^2\). The only integer square strictly between these two squares is \(q^2\). Consequently, \(P\) can be a square in this range only when \(30-3x=0\), giving \(x=10\). This value works: \(q=131\) and \(P=131^2\).

It remains to check \(x=-6,-5,-4,-3,-2,-1,0,1,2\). Their corresponding values of \(P\), in that order, are
\[
409,166,67,40,37,34,31,52,145.
\]
None is a square, as the following consecutive-square comparisons show:
\[
\begin{gathered}
20^2<409<21^2,\\
12^2<145<166<13^2,\\
8^2<67<9^2,\\
6^2<37<40<7^2,\\
5^2<31<34<6^2,\\
7^2<52<8^2.
\end{gathered}
\]
These disjoint ranges cover every integer \(x\), and only \(x=10\) works. Therefore \(\boxed{n=1}\), choice \(\mathrm D\).
solutions.title: Compare with nearby squares
